profile.title: Physical Layer
profile.subject: Academic Course Material

topics.name: Physical Layer Function
topics.description: The physical layer is the first and lowest layer of the OSI model and is responsible for carrying bits across a physical transmission medium.

topics.name: Analog and Digital Signals
topics.description: An analog signal varies continuously and smoothly over time, whereas a digital signal uses discrete values, commonly represented as LOW and HIGH or 0 and 1.

topics.name: Bit Rate and Bit Length
topics.description: Bit rate is the number of bits transmitted per second, while bit length is the physical distance occupied by one bit in a medium. Higher bit rates pack more bits into a given transmission distance.

topics.name: Physical Layer and Signal Fundamentals
topics.description: Explains the physical layer's role in carrying bits and introduces the basic forms and measurements of transmitted signals.

topics.name: Digital Modulation and Encoding Assumptions
topics.description: Digital modulation converts bits into signals and received signals back into bits. The introductory model assumes discrete high and low signals for encoding binary 1 and 0.

topics.name: Non-Return to Zero and Desynchronization
topics.description: Non-Return to Zero represents 1 with a high signal and 0 with a low signal. Long sequences without transitions make receiver clock recovery difficult and can cause desynchronization.

topics.name: Non-Return to Zero Inverted
topics.description: NRZI represents a binary 1 by making a signal transition and a binary 0 by leaving the signal unchanged.

topics.name: Manchester Encoding
topics.description: Manchester encoding uses a high-to-low transition for 1 and a low-to-high transition for 0, providing regular transitions that support clock synchronization.

topics.name: 4-bit/5-bit Encoding
topics.description: The 4-bit/5-bit technique maps four-bit data groups into five-bit codes to prevent problematic sequences of zeros when used with NRZI, including in 100 Mbps Ethernet.

topics.name: Differential Encoding Strategies
topics.description: Differential encoding represents data through changes in signal state rather than relying only on absolute voltage levels.

topics.name: Digital Data Encoding Techniques
topics.description: Examines how binary data is converted into physical signals and the synchronization properties of major line-encoding methods.

topics.name: Asynchronous Transmission
topics.description: Asynchronous transmission sends data as individual bytes or characters, with timing established separately for each transmitted unit.

topics.name: Synchronous Transmission
topics.description: Synchronous transmission sends data in blocks or frames using coordinated timing between the sender and receiver.

topics.name: Asynchronous and Synchronous Transmission
topics.description: Compares character-oriented asynchronous transmission with block- or frame-oriented synchronous transmission.

topics.name: Transmission Impairment Overview
topics.description: Transmission impairments are effects that degrade signals as they pass through a medium, principally attenuation, distortion, and noise.

topics.name: Attenuation
topics.description: Attenuation is the loss of signal energy as a signal travels through a transmission medium, resulting in a weaker received signal.

topics.name: Distortion
topics.description: Distortion occurs when a signal changes its form or shape, particularly when components of a composite signal propagate differently.

topics.name: Noise
topics.description: Noise is unwanted energy that interferes with a signal during transmission. The material introduces multiple noise types, including thermal noise caused by random electron motion.

topics.name: Transmission Impairments
topics.description: Describes attenuation, distortion, and noise as factors that reduce the quality of a transmitted signal.

topics.name: Analog and Digital Signal Applications
topics.description: Applied examples examine continuous temperature measurements, analog and IP cameras, Internet data carried over radio waves, digitally transmitted information, and analog radio systems.

topics.name: Frequency and Bit Rate Measurement
topics.description: Hertz measures frequency or cycles per second, while bits per second measures the rate at which binary data is transmitted.

topics.name: Applied Signal Analysis
topics.description: Uses practical questions to distinguish analog and digital signals and clarify the quantities measured by hertz and bits per second.

topics.name: Nyquist Formula
topics.description: The Nyquist formula determines the maximum bit rate of a noiseless channel from its bandwidth and number of discrete signal levels: Maximum Bit Rate = 2B log2 L.

topics.name: Shannon Formula
topics.description: The Shannon formula determines channel capacity in the presence of noise using bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio: Channel Capacity = B log2(1 + SNR).

topics.name: Maximum Bit Rate and Channel Capacity
topics.description: Introduces formulas for determining theoretical transmission limits in noiseless and noisy channels.

topics.name: Guided and Unguided Transmission Media
topics.description: Transmission media provide the path over which signals travel and are classified into guided media, which constrain signals to a physical path, and unguided media, which transmit through free space.

topics.name: Classes of Transmission Medium
topics.description: Introduces transmission media as resources below and directly controlled by the physical layer and divides them into guided and unguided classes.

topics.name: Twisted Pair Cable
topics.description: Twisted-pair cable contains two individually insulated conductors, usually copper. Its applications include telephone lines and low-cost LANs, and its forms include Unshielded Twisted Pair and shielded variants.

topics.name: Coaxial Cable
topics.description: Coaxial cable uses concentric conductors and carries higher-frequency signals than twisted pair. It provides higher bandwidth and strong noise immunity for communication applications.

topics.name: Fibre Optic Cable and Propagation Modes
topics.description: Fibre-optic cable uses a glass or plastic core and transmits information as light. Its propagation modes depend on the core and lower-density cladding, and the medium offers high bandwidth and low attenuation alongside stated disadvantages and applications.

topics.name: Guided Transmission Media
topics.description: Examines twisted-pair, coaxial, and fibre-optic cables as bounded media for signal transmission.

topics.name: Wireless Propagation Methods
topics.description: Unguided transmission uses electromagnetic waves traveling through free space. Propagation methods include ground propagation, in which lower-frequency radio waves follow the curvature of the Earth.

topics.name: Radio Waves
topics.description: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves in the approximate frequency range of 3 kHz to 1 GHz and are used for wireless communication.

topics.name: Microwaves
topics.description: Microwaves occupy the approximate frequency range from 1 GHz to 300 GHz and are used as an unguided communication medium.

topics.name: Infrared
topics.description: Infrared communication uses frequencies of approximately 300 GHz to 400 THz and is suited to short-range communication.

topics.name: Unguided Transmission Media
topics.description: Explains wireless propagation methods and the frequency ranges and communication properties of radio waves, microwaves, and infrared.

topics.name: Applied Channel Capacity and Fibre Propagation Analysis
topics.description: Review questions distinguish Nyquist and Shannon parameters and examine single-mode and multimode fibre, modal dispersion in step-index fibre, dispersion reduction in graded-index fibre, and total internal reflection.

topics.name: Channel Capacity and Optical Fibre Review
topics.description: Applies channel-capacity principles and compares optical-fibre propagation modes, modal dispersion, graded-index behavior, and total internal reflection.

topics.name: Switching Networks and Switching Methods
topics.description: A switching network is a collection of interconnected nodes and connections used for communication. Data can be switched using circuit switching or packet switching, with packet switching divided into datagram and virtual-circuit approaches.

topics.name: Switching Network Foundations
topics.description: Defines a switching network and identifies the principal methods used to move data through interconnected nodes.

topics.name: Circuit Switching
topics.description: Circuit switching establishes a dedicated communication path through circuit establishment, data transfer, and circuit disconnection phases. It can be inefficient because channel capacity remains dedicated for the connection's duration.

topics.name: Packet Switching
topics.description: Packet switching divides a long message into packets and sends the packets through the network individually, allowing network resources to be shared.

topics.name: Datagram Packet Switching
topics.description: Datagram switching is connectionless: no route is established before transmission, and individual packets may be handled independently.

topics.name: Virtual Circuit Packet Switching
topics.description: Virtual-circuit switching establishes a planned route before packets are sent, providing a connection-oriented path for the packet sequence.

topics.name: Applied Comparison of Switching Methods
topics.description: Review questions evaluate virtual-circuit behavior, the inefficiency of idle dedicated circuits, and the greater resource efficiency generally provided by packet switching.

topics.name: Circuit and Packet Switching
topics.description: Explains the operation, organization, and resource-use characteristics of circuit-switched and packet-switched communication.
